newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan welcomes U.S. renewal of China MFN status.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan welcomes U.S. renewal of China MFN status.

text.p: Taiwan on Tuesday welcomed Washington's plan to renew Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trade status for China, saying the move would benefit 30,000 Taiwan firms with investments in the communist mainland.
"This is a very good development for Taiwan businessmen investing in the mainland," Chen Ruey-long, deputy director of the cabinet's Board of Foreign Trade, said on state radio.
"Mainland China's MFN status will help Taiwan businessmen expand in the U.S. market," Chen said.

Some 30,000 Taiwan firms have poured more than US$30 billion into the mainland despite a bitter rivalry dating to 1949, when a civil war left the mainland in communist control and Taiwan in the hands of the defeated Chinese Nationalists.
The United States is the main market for many Taiwan-funded companies operating in the mainland, Chen added.

U.S. President Bill Clinton said on Monday he had decided to accord China what amounts to normal trade tariff status for the coming year despite disagreements with Beijing on many issues, notably its human rights record.
Washington denies MFN only to Afghanistan, Cuba, Laos, North Korea, Serbia and Vietnam. Iran, Iraq and Libya technically enjoy MFN status but are subject to trade embargoes.

The move to renew China's MFN status, an annual decision that every president has made since 1980, was expected to be controversial in Congress, where some legislators pledged to try to reverse Clinton's decision.
Taiwan's economics vice minister Sheu Ke-sheng said China's MFN extension would have no direct impact on Taiwan's economy. He did not elaborate.
Taiwan still bans all direct contact and investment on the mainland, obliging all government-approved China investments to be routed through Hong Kong or other third places.

Due to festering political strains, Taiwan still bans major infrastructural investments in China and seeks to limit its overall investment so that the island does not become overly dependent on its main rival -- and thus politically vulnerable.
